PairCover-Q: presentation speech

About 10 minutes. Updated 28 Oct 2026 with the real IBM hardware run. Blue boxes = what to say. Yellow boxes = what to click or show.

1. Opening and the problem (1 min)

Show the Home page. Let the animation play.

Good evening sir, we are Team Evric, and our project is PairCover-Q. It is about ambulance dispatch.

Normally the dispatcher sends the nearest free ambulance to each emergency. That works for one call. But when several calls come at the same time, sending the nearest ambulance to every call can leave a whole area with no backup.

In this animation, A1 and A2 cover the same area for each other. Nearest-available sends both of them, so that area is empty, and the cost is 22. Our method keeps A2 at home and sends A3 to the second call. One call waits one minute longer, but the area stays protected, and the cost is 13.

2. How we model it (2 min)

Scroll to "How it works" on the Home page (three cards).

We turn this into a math problem. For every choice "does ambulance A go to call C", we make one yes/no variable. That is one qubit.

Our cost has three parts: priority-weighted response time, a penalty if a call is left unserved, and a pairwise penalty that switches on only when two backup partners both leave. That last term is a product of exactly two variables, so the whole problem is a QUBO, which is the form that quantum optimisers accept. We need no extra qubits for the coverage rule.

Then we solve the same problem three ways: the nearest-ambulance rule, an exact brute-force search, and QAOA in Qiskit, on a simulator and on a real IBM quantum computer. Every quantum answer is checked against the exact answer and against random guessing.

3. Live demo: the dispatch console (2 min)

Open Try it, then Dispatch console. Click "Compare nearest vs exact". If time allows, open "Create your own emergency", click the map to place calls, and run it.

This is our dispatch console. On the left are the waiting calls and the available ambulances. In the middle is the response zone, where the dashed lines are travel minutes and the shaded pill is the backup pair A1 and A2.

I'll run nearest-available and then the exact optimiser, and the console explains what changed: the exact plan keeps A2 home and the cost falls from 22 to 13.

4. Classical vs quantum, on a real IBM quantum computer (3 min)

Open Quantum, then Classical vs Quantum. Start on "4 qubits · depth 2". Point at the four timing cards, then the table, then the bar chart. Then click "6 qubits · depth 2" and show that the chip falls below guessing.

Our mentor asked us to show classical and quantum side by side, and to run on real hardware. This page does both, on one dispatch problem.

The first two rows are classical: the nearest-ambulance rule and an exact search over every option. They run live, in well under a millisecond. The third row is QAOA on a noiseless simulator, also live. The next row is the same circuit run on ibm_fez, a real 156-qubit IBM quantum processor, in IBM job dbh0tjpt9uhs73c960mg on 28 October. The last rows are IBM's noise copies of the same chip.

On this 4-qubit problem, the answer the real chip gave most often is the best dispatch, A3 to call 1, the same as the exact solver. It hit the best plan in 27.7 percent of shots. Random guessing among valid plans gets 20 percent, so the chip is about 1.4 times better than guessing. In the noiseless simulator it was 59 percent, so noise took away about half of the gain.

Now the latency. The classical answer takes a fraction of a millisecond. The quantum job took 12 and a half minutes end to end: almost 3 minutes in the queue and about 10 minutes of processing. The circuits themselves ran on the chip for only 3.2 seconds, using 5 seconds of our free 10 minutes a month.

Now the 6-qubit problem. After mapping onto the chip the circuit has 82 two-qubit gates, and at that size the real chip finds the best plan only 5.2 percent of the time, below the 6.7 percent of guessing. So today's hardware helps only at the very smallest sizes. Notice also that here the nearest-ambulance rule picks a worse plan than the exact solver, because it ignores coverage. That is the point of our method.

5. Results, with honest limits (1.5 min)

Open About, then Evidence. Show the chart, then switch to the "QAOA benchmark" tab.

One example is not enough, so we ran a simulation: a synthetic 24 by 24 km city, 7 ambulances, calls arriving over 7 days, repeated 30 times at each load.

At 5 calls per hour, mean response time fell by 2.15 minutes compared with nearest-available. Most of this comes from planning simultaneous calls together: batching alone gives 2.18 minutes. The coverage term's own contribution is less uncovered demand, with no significant change in late arrivals.

For QAOA, we benchmarked 23 problems of 4 to 12 qubits. With a good starting strategy at depth 3, QAOA beat random guessing among valid plans on 19 of 23 problems in simulation. The hardware run you just saw shows how noise eats into that gain.

So we do not claim quantum advantage. A normal computer solves these in milliseconds. What we show is a complete quantum pipeline, from an emergency to a QUBO to a circuit on real IBM hardware and back to a dispatch decision, checked at every step against the exact answer.

6. Roadmap (1 min)

We now know where the hardware stops helping for our encoding: between 4 and 6 qubits. Our next steps attack exactly that.

  1. Error mitigation on the hardware runs: dynamical decoupling, readout correction and twirling, which IBM Runtime offers directly.
  2. A feasibility-preserving XY mixer, because on the real chip only 45 percent of samples were valid plans.
  3. Shallower circuits and angles tuned on the device, instead of angles tuned only in simulation.
  4. Repeated hardware runs on several days and devices, to give error bars.
  5. Larger fleets, where exact search stops being instant, which is where a quantum solver could start to matter.

If the judges ask...

  • "Is this faster than classical?" No. Exact search takes under a millisecond; the hardware path took 12.5 minutes. We claim a validated pipeline and a measured path, not speed.
  • "Did you really run on hardware?" Yes: ibm_fez, IBM Heron r2, 156 qubits, job dbh0tjpt9uhs73c960mg on 28 Oct 2026, 4,096 shots per circuit. The raw counts are in reports/ibm_hardware in our repository.
  • "Why does the real chip do worse than the fake backend?" The fake backend copies an old calibration snapshot. The real chip has drift and crosstalk the copy leaves out, so we treat fake-backend numbers as optimistic.
  • "How many qubits does a real problem need?" One per eligible ambulance-call pair. Most real decisions are 2 qubits; 8 or more only when several calls arrive together.
  • "Why QAOA?" The problem is naturally a QUBO, and QAOA is the standard hybrid algorithm for QUBOs on near-term devices.
  • "Is the data real?" No, everything is synthetic and labelled that way. We have no real ambulance records.
  • "Why is the penalty set just above the bound?" Bigger penalties make almost every sample valid but flatten the differences between plans, so the best one is harder to find. Our sweep showed 2.16x at the tight penalty against 0.62x at 4x.
  • "If you don't know": "We have not tested that yet; it is on our roadmap."
